endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Regularly evaluate GAI system vulnerabilities to possible circumvention of safety measures.

evidence.title: Patient Perceptions and preferences for the disclosure of artificial intelligence generated draft replies to electronic messages - A qualitative study
evidence.outcome: Understanding of AI content origin disclosure
evidence.effect: Nearly half of 30 participants were unable to identify AI as the draft's writer.
evidence.quote: Patient interpretations of disclosure statements suggested that written disclosure statements did not provide sufficient information to clarify how AI was used, with nearly half of participants unable to identify AI as the draft's writer.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether evaluating user understanding of AI provenance labels, with feedback analyzed by literacy level, improves understanding or reduces misattribution of AI-generated content. One small simulated study found that nearly half of 30 adult portal users could not identify AI as the writer of a draft, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that this evaluation practice corrects it.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is qualitative, simulated, and small (n=30). It documents misunderstanding of AI origin disclosure but provides no comparison of deployers who evaluate label comprehension against those who do not.

In a simulated portal setting, nearly half of 30 participants did not recognize that AI wrote the draft. Patients who believe a clinician wrote a message may give it more weight than they would give machine text. Comprehension testing could surface this failure before deployment, though no study shows that it prevents harm.

The hazard study does not report participant literacy, language, or insurance status, so it cannot show whether misunderstanding differs by literacy level. The recommendation's call to stratify feedback by literacy addresses a plausible gap, but no data yet describe how low-literacy or limited English proficiency patients read provenance labels.

The only endorsement, NIST AI 600-1, asks deployers to evaluate vulnerabilities to circumvention of safety measures. That language supports periodic evaluation in general but does not name provenance label comprehension or literacy stratification. The link between the endorsement and this specific practice is indirect.

Nearly half of participants in one study could not tell that AI had written a portal draft. Patients have a stake in knowing who wrote what they read. Asking patients whether labels make sense is a direct way to check this, though its effect on trust and understanding has not been measured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare label designs or comprehension-testing programs against usual practice in live patient portals, measure correct identification of AI authorship as the outcome, and report results stratified by health literacy and preferred language.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study of 30 United States adult portal users did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or literacy characteristics. As a result, there is no evidence on how these populations interpret AI provenance labels or whether literacy-stratified evaluation would detect differences.
